# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

When you search text for a living, you spend a lot of energy narrowing *where*
to look. ripgrep's file-type filters let you name a set of files once — "Rust
files," "C files," "web files" — and reuse that name instead of retyping globs.
This guide covers the four flags you'll use most: `--type`, `--type-not`,
`--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## What a "type" is

A file type is just a name assigned to one or more globs that match the
relevant files. That's the whole idea. The `rust` type is a name for `*.rs`;
the `c` type covers both C source and headers so you don't have to write
`-g '*.{c,h}'` by hand. ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types,
generally corresponding to well-known public formats.

One detail worth internalizing: type globs are matched against the **file name
only**, not the full path. A type also never applies to directories. So a type
like `sh` (which is defined by extension globs) will not match an
extensionless script named `my-shell-script`.

## `--type` (`-t`): only search this type

`--type TYPE` limits ripgrep to files matching `TYPE`. Search for `fn run` in
Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust      # short form; -t and the value can be joined
```

You can pass `--type` multiple times to include several types at once
(`-trust -tpython` searches both).

`--type` accepts the special value `all`, which behaves as if you'd passed
`--type` for *every* type ripgrep knows about, including any you added on the
command line. `--type=all` therefore puts ripgrep in "whitelist" mode: it
searches only files it recognizes via its type definitions.

Precedence matters. `--type` has **lower precedence than the `--glob` (`-g`)
flag and than any rules found in ignore files**. Type filtering narrows what
ripgrep already considers searchable; it does not override an explicit glob or
a `.gitignore` rule.

## `--type-not` (`-T`): skip this type

`--type-not TYPE` is the inverse: do not search files matching `TYPE`.

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type." You can mix them freely on one command line
(`-Trust -ttoml -Tjson`), and when a file matches conflicting type globs, the
**last matching glob wins**.

`--type-not` also accepts `all`. `--type-not=all` is "blacklist" mode: ripgrep
searches only files that are *unrecognized* by its type definitions. This is
the natural complement to `--type=all` — for example, `--type-not=all` would
search the extensionless `my-shell-script` that `--type=all` skips.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

`--type-list` prints every supported file type and its globs, one type per
line, as `name: glob, glob, ...`. Pipe it through ripgrep itself to inspect a
single type:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

Importantly, `--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags
given on the same command line, so it's the way to confirm a custom definition
took effect.

## `--type-add`: define your own types

`--type-add` adds a new glob for a type using the form `TYPE:GLOB`. Only one
glob is added at a time, but you can repeat the flag. Suppose you often search
"web" files — JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title      # same thing, condensed
```

Unless you use `--type-clear` first, new globs are *added* to any existing
globs for that type. Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or
numbers — no punctuation.

`--type-add` also supports an `include` directive that imports the rules of
other, already-defined types. To build a `src` type covering C++, Python, and
Markdown, then extend it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc TODO
```

### These settings are not saved

`--type-add` (and `--type-clear`) apply only to the current invocation.
Nothing is persisted. To make a custom type available everywhere, pass it on
every run via a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add a line to your ripgrep configuration file:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Quick reference

- `-t TYPE` / `--type` — search only this type; `all` = whitelist mode.
- `-T TYPE` / `--type-not` — skip this type; `all` = blacklist mode.
- `--type-add 'name:glob'` — define/extend a type (or `name:include:a,b`);
  not persisted.
- `--type-list` — list all types and their globs, honoring your additions.
